transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
President Trump has arrived in China for a rare three-way meeting with Russian President
Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
The talks are set to take place in southern China, where Xi and Putin spoke at an Asia-Pacific
economic summit.
He is calling for open trade, while Putin is criticizing Western sanctions.
Earlier today, Trump met with the leader of the Philippines, as NPR's Deepa Shivaram
reports.
Trump and the U.S. delegation visited the presidential palace in Manila.
With Secretary of State Marco Rubio seated beside him, Trump reaffirmed the U.S. relationship
with the Philippines.
With this visit, we're building on these ties to make our partnership even closer.
Trump said the two countries were working to improve energy security and expand defense
cooperation.
The president also briefly talked about U.S. actions abroad, saying the U.S. is, quote,
"doing very well in Iran," despite the conflict going on months longer than Trump said it
would.
He also spoke of U.S. intervention in Venezuela, calling it a, quote, "acquisition."
Deepa Shivaram, NPR News, Shenzhen, China.
The president's trip comes amid a string of technical disruptions in the United States.
An FAA outage grounded flights nationwide on Friday.
There have also been problems with Microsoft and disruptions to banking services this week.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who's traveling with the president, says the administration
is treating them as separate incidents.
We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances
have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another
nation state, with a malign actor of any kind.
Again, we have no evidence of that.
We have no indications of that.
We have no reason to believe that.
One of those outages left some bank customers unable to get into their accounts on Monday.
JPMorgan Chase says a software bug caused the disruption, which also affected the money
transfer service, Zell.
The White House has withdrawn Dr. Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration.
NPR's Cindy Lupkin reports a Senate committee had been set to vote on the nomination this
morning.
Senators waited nearly two months to vote on Overton after hearing about her qualifications.
And now they won't get the chance.
Louisiana Republican Senator Bill Cassidy, who chairs the health committee, said he was
still undecided on CBS's Face the Nation on Sunday.
Meanwhile, many advocacy groups and medical professionals said they opposed her confirmation.
Here's Dr. Robert Steinbruch, a public citizen.
She just hasn't made a convincing case for herself.
There are concerns about what she has to say about the safety of vaccines, about the safety
of medication abortion, about the safety of vapes and flavored e-cigarettes.
She questioned her ability to follow the science and to manage the 18,000-person agency.
Sydney Lupkin, NPR News.
Stocks in Asia are mixed today.
Markets in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan are trading higher, while shares are down in Shanghai.
This is NPR.
The Associated Press has called the U.S. Senate race in Alaska for Democrat Mary Peltola.
The former Congresswoman defeated Republican Senator Dan Sullivan more than two weeks after
the midterm elections.
Liz Ruskin from Alaska Public Media reports.
Peltola ran on the national Democratic themes of affordability and against corruption.
She also said Alaska would fight corporate greed to get its fish back, a reference to
an at-sea fishing industry that intercepts Alaska salmon.
That's Liz Ruskin from Alaska Public Media reporting.
Waymo has temporarily stopped freeway operations of its driverless cars nationwide.
That's after the California DMV restricted the company's freeway use over safety concerns.
Azul Dostrom Ekman from member station KQED in San Francisco reports.
The order's been in effect since last week.
The California DMV says Waymo's freeway operations posed a "imminent hazard" to public safety.
That's after several recent incidents, including one where three Waymo robo-taxis entered an
active construction closure on a freeway in the San Francisco Bay Area.
In a statement, Waymo said it halted freeway operations in other markets, like in Phoenix,
Arizona and Los Angeles, while its vehicles continue to operate on surface streets.
The DMV's order will be in place until Waymo provides evidence that it's corrected the
issue.
For NPR News, I'm Azul Dostrom Ekman in San Francisco.
I'm Windsor Johnston, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Trump arrives in China for three-way meeting with Putin and Xi Jinping
Trump meets Philippine leader in Manila, reaffirms ties and defense cooperation
FAA outage grounds flights nationwide, with Microsoft and banking disruptions this week
JPMorgan Chase blames software bug for bank customers locked out of accounts
White House withdraws Dr. Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration
Asian stock markets mixed, with Japan, South Korea and Taiwan higher
AP calls Alaska Senate race for Democrat Mary Peltola over Republican Dan Sullivan
California DMV halts Waymo freeway driverless operations nationwide over safety concerns
